explanation: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4), then all queued microtasks drain completely (3, the Promise callback), and only then does the next macrotask (2, the timer) run.

promptText: Which script attribute downloads in parallel with HTML parsing but executes only after parsing completes, in document order?
options: defer
async
neither attribute changes execution timing
async and defer behave identically in every browser
explanation: defer downloads without blocking parsing and executes after parsing finishes, in document order; async also downloads in parallel but executes as soon as it's ready, out of order, and can still interrupt parsing.

promptText: A developer sees a CORS error and tries to add a header from React code running in the browser to fix it. Why doesn't this work?
options: CORS is enforced by the browser based on headers the server sends back; only the server can grant the permission via its own response headers
CORS errors only occur for GET requests, and this fix is only invalid for POST
React automatically strips any custom header set from application code before a request is sent
CORS is a build-time setting configured in package.json, not a runtime browser behavior
explanation: The Same-Origin Policy and CORS are enforced entirely by the browser based on the server's response headers — a frontend cannot grant itself permission to read a cross-origin response; the fix always lives on the server.

promptText: What is the key security tradeoff between storing an auth token in localStorage versus an httpOnly cookie?
options: localStorage is readable by any JS on the page (vulnerable to XSS theft) but immune to CSRF since it isn't auto-attached; an httpOnly cookie is invisible to JS but is sent automatically, requiring SameSite/CSRF defenses
httpOnly cookies are always slower to read than localStorage, with no security difference
A localStorage token expires automatically when the browser restarts, while cookies never expire
There is no meaningful security difference between the two storage mechanisms
explanation: It's a genuine tradeoff between two threat models: localStorage trades CSRF-immunity for full XSS exposure, while an httpOnly cookie trades XSS-read-immunity for needing SameSite/CSRF-token defenses since the browser attaches it automatically.

promptText: Why do animating transform and opacity avoid both the reflow and repaint costs that animating width or top would incur?
options: Transform/opacity changes can be handled at the compositing stage alone (often GPU-accelerated) without recomputing layout geometry or repainting pixels
The browser completely ignores transform and opacity properties during any animation
Changes to width and top are automatically cached and reused by the rendering engine
CSS transitions bypass the JavaScript engine entirely, making all CSS transitions free
explanation: Compositing-only changes like transform and opacity skip both layout recalculation and repainting, making them the cheapest category of visual update, unlike width/top which trigger a full reflow.

promptText: Which statement about a Service Worker is accurate?
options: It runs on its own background thread as a network proxy with no direct DOM access
It runs on the main thread and can directly call document.querySelector to manipulate the DOM
It makes a manifest.json entirely unnecessary for a Progressive Web App to be installable
It can intercept only GET requests and is structurally unable to see POST requests
explanation: A Service Worker runs on a separate thread, acting as a programmable network proxy that intercepts fetch events, but it has no access to the DOM at all — that access lives only on the page.

promptText: A synchronous <script> tag in <head> blocks HTML parsing, yet its network download often starts immediately anyway, before the parser even reaches it. Why?
options: A preload scanner runs ahead of the main parser looking only for resource URLs and kicks off fetches early, so "parser-blocking" and "network-blocking" are different things
Browsers always download every script referenced anywhere on the page the instant the HTML response begins, regardless of any blocking behavior
The browser silently retries the script request three times before actually blocking the parser
Scripts placed in <head> are never actually render- or parser-blocking; only scripts in <body> are
explanation: The lightweight preload scanner speculatively scans upcoming markup for resource URLs and starts fetches before the main parser reaches them, hiding network latency even though execution still blocks parsing.

promptText: Using font-display: swap avoids a flash of invisible text (FOIT). What new problem can it introduce instead?
options: Layout shift (hurting CLS) when the fallback font and the web font have different metrics, causing text to reflow once the web font finishes loading
It permanently disables downloading of the actual web font, using only the fallback forever
It disables font hinting and anti-aliasing across the entire page
It forces every font on the page to render in a single shared fallback typeface
explanation: swap shows a fallback immediately (avoiding FOIT) but swaps in the web font once ready — if the fallback and web font have different metrics, that swap causes a layout shift, which is why font-metric-override techniques exist to compensate.

promptText: A page's Largest Contentful Paint element is a large hero image marked with loading="lazy". Why does this hurt LCP?
options: Lazy-loading is meant to defer below-the-fold images; applying it to the LCP element delays its discovery and fetch, directly pushing back the exact metric it should help elsewhere
loading="lazy" silently disables image compression, increasing the file's transfer size
Lazy-loaded images are always rendered at a lower resolution by the browser
LCP is calculated purely from text content, so image loading strategy has no effect on it
explanation: loading="lazy" on the LCP element is a classic anti-pattern — it delays the very resource that determines the metric; the LCP image should instead be discoverable in the initial HTML and preloaded with fetchpriority="high".

promptText: Given the header Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=3600, stale-while-revalidate=86400, how does a browser's cache behave differently from a CDN's shared cache?
options: The browser treats the response fresh for only 60 seconds while the CDN/shared cache treats it fresh for a full hour, decoupling browser freshness from edge freshness
The browser ignores s-maxage entirely and always caches the response for 86400 seconds
The CDN ignores max-age and instead caches the response for exactly 60 seconds, same as the browser
stale-while-revalidate overrides both max-age and s-maxage, making them irrelevant
explanation: max-age governs any cache including the browser, while s-maxage specifically overrides that duration for shared/CDN caches, letting you cache longer at the edge than in an individual browser.

promptText: Why is domain sharding (splitting assets across fake subdomains like static1.example.com, static2.example.com) now considered an anti-pattern under HTTP/2+?
options: A single HTTP/2 connection already multiplexes many parallel streams, so sharding just adds extra DNS lookups and TLS handshakes per shard without the old HTTP/1.1 parallelism benefit
Domain sharding was never effective under any version of the HTTP protocol, including HTTP/1.1
HTTP/2 technically forbids browsers from ever connecting to more than one subdomain per page
Browsers now cap the total number of connections per page regardless of how many domains are used, making sharding a protocol violation
explanation: Domain sharding was a legitimate workaround for HTTP/1.1's per-host connection cap; HTTP/2's multiplexing removes that ceiling, so the extra DNS/TLS overhead of sharding now actively hurts performance instead of helping.

promptText: Why is SharedArrayBuffer restricted to cross-origin-isolated pages that send COOP and COEP headers?
options: Unrestricted shared memory combined with high-resolution timing enabled a practical Spectre side-channel attack, so browsers require strict cross-origin isolation before re-enabling it
SharedArrayBuffer was fully deprecated, and COOP/COEP are the mechanism to explicitly opt back into a removed API
It is purely a browser-vendor licensing requirement with no technical security basis
COOP and COEP headers are required for all JavaScript execution on any page, not specifically for SharedArrayBuffer
explanation: Browsers broadly disabled SharedArrayBuffer after Spectre was disclosed because shared, precisely-timed memory enabled a real side-channel attack, and only re-enabled it under the strict cross-origin isolation guaranteed by COOP+COEP.

promptText: A developer assumes the structured clone algorithm (used by postMessage) is "just like JSON.stringify but for workers," and therefore strictly weaker in capability. Where exactly is that assumption wrong?
options: Structured clone correctly handles circular references, unlike JSON.stringify which throws on them, and it can also clone Maps, Sets, Dates, and ArrayBuffers that JSON.stringify cannot represent at all
JSON.stringify can clone functions and DOM nodes while structured clone cannot clone anything but plain objects
Structured clone is strictly slower than JSON.stringify in every case with no other functional difference
JSON.stringify supports Transferable objects for zero-copy messaging, while structured clone does not
explanation: Structured clone is actually more capable than JSON.stringify in specific ways — notably handling circular references correctly and supporting richer built-in types — which is a common correction to offer when someone implies it's strictly the weaker option.

promptText: In the Performance tab's flamechart, a developer looks only at the single widest bar and concludes it's the bottleneck, missing a function that's individually cheap but called 10,000 times. What view in the same panel would have caught this, and why?
options: The "Bottom-Up" (aggregated self-time) view, because it sums total time spent across every invocation of a function rather than showing only the single largest individual call
The Network tab's waterfall, because network requests always dominate CPU-bound bottlenecks regardless of call frequency
The Memory tab's heap snapshot comparison, because memory usage and CPU time are measured identically in DevTools
There is no way to detect this pattern in browser DevTools; only a server-side profiler can find it
explanation: A cost spread across many small invocations can dominate total time despite never appearing as one wide bar in the flamechart; the Bottom-Up/Call Tree views aggregate self-time across all calls to the same function, surfacing exactly this pattern.

promptText: A team obsesses over reaching a perfect Lighthouse score in CI but ships a page real users report as janky to interact with. What gap in Lighthouse's methodology explains this disconnect?
options: Lighthouse produces lab data from a single simulated run and cannot meaningfully measure Interaction to Next Paint (INP) at all — it only reports Total Blocking Time as a lab proxy — so real responsiveness requires field data (CrUX/RUM) across actual varied user interactions
Lighthouse scores are generated without any real measurement and carry no signal about performance whatsoever
INP is not a genuine performance metric, only a marketing term with no technical definition
A perfect Lighthouse score mathematically guarantees zero real-user interaction jank by definition
explanation: Lab data like Lighthouse is a single, controlled, reproducible run useful for debugging but not representative of real users, and it structurally cannot measure INP since that depends on varied real interaction patterns — field data is what actually reflects user experience.
